passages.author: Julius Caesar
passages.title: Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.1
passages.source: Public-domain Caesar text prepared as a hand-corrected MVP sample; intended to be replaceable by Perseus/Scaife CTS imports.
passages.description: Caesar opens the Gallic War by making geography feel like evidence: peoples, borders, rivers, and political distance all become part of the argument.

sentences.latin: Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres.
sentences.translation: All Gaul is divided into three parts.
sentences.syntaxExplanation: The subject is Gallia, modified by omnis. Est divisa forms a perfect passive periphrasis-like predicate, while in partes tres expresses the result of the division.

tokens.contextMeaning: The whole region of Gaul, not merely one tribe.
tokens.grammarNote: The nominative marks the thing being described. Caesar treats a complex region as one grammatical subject before subdividing it.
tokens.etymology: Latin Gallia is built from Galli, the Roman name for the Gauls.

tokens.contextMeaning: Serves as the finite verb linking the subject to the passive participle.
tokens.grammarNote: With a perfect passive participle, est can describe a resulting state: Gaul stands divided.
tokens.etymology: From Proto-Indo-European *h1es-, the same deep root behind English is.

tokens.contextMeaning: Emphasizes the total region under discussion.
tokens.grammarNote: Omnis agrees with Gallia in case, number, and gender. The word order Gallia est omnis places emphasis on the totality.
tokens.etymology: An old Latin adjective for totality; related forms appear throughout Roman legal and historical prose.

tokens.morphology: perfect passive participle, nominative singular feminine
tokens.contextMeaning: Describes Gaul as already partitioned into distinct regions.
tokens.grammarNote: The participle agrees with Gallia. Its passive force matters: Gaul is not doing the dividing; it is represented as divided.
tokens.etymology: From dis- plus a root related to separating or apportioning.

tokens.contextMeaning: Introduces the resulting parts of the division.
tokens.grammarNote: With the accusative, in often indicates motion or result into a state or category.
tokens.etymology: A very old Indo-European preposition with spatial and metaphorical uses.

tokens.contextMeaning: The divisions Caesar will immediately name.
tokens.grammarNote: The accusative plural is required by in in this result-oriented phrase.
tokens.etymology: Related to Latin partior, to divide or share.

tokens.contextMeaning: The exact number of divisions in Caesar's opening taxonomy.
tokens.grammarNote: Tres agrees with partes in gender and case. Numerals one through three decline in Latin.
tokens.etymology: Cognate with English three and Greek treis.

sentences.latin: Harum unam incolunt Belgae, aliam Aquitani, tertiam qui ipsorum lingua Celtae, nostra Galli appellantur.
sentences.translation: Of these, the Belgae inhabit one part, the Aquitani another, and the third those who in their own language are called Celtae, in ours Galli.
sentences.syntaxExplanation: Harum is a partitive genitive pointing back to partes. Unam, aliam, and tertiam organize the three divisions. The relative clause qui ... appellantur identifies the people of the third part by two names.

tokens.contextMeaning: Refers back to the three partes.
tokens.grammarNote: A partitive genitive marks the larger set from which one item is selected.
tokens.etymology: From the Latin hic demonstrative family, used for things near in discourse.

tokens.contextMeaning: One of the three regions.
tokens.grammarNote: Unam stands substantively: one part. Its feminine gender follows partes.
tokens.etymology: Cognate with English one through Indo-European ancestry.

tokens.contextMeaning: Caesar assigns peoples to territory.
tokens.syntaxRole: Main verb of the first clause.
tokens.grammarNote: The plural ending -unt agrees with Belgae, the plural subject.
tokens.etymology: From in- plus colo, to cultivate, dwell, or inhabit.

tokens.contextMeaning: A northern confederation presented as one of the major Gallic groups.
tokens.grammarNote: The nominative plural marks the inhabitants doing the action.
tokens.etymology: A Roman ethnonym for peoples in northern Gaul.

tokens.contextMeaning: A second part, inhabited by the Aquitani.
tokens.grammarNote: Latin often omits repeated verbs when the parallel structure is clear.
tokens.etymology: From an old pronominal stem meaning other.

tokens.contextMeaning: The people of southwestern Gaul.
tokens.grammarNote: Caesar relies on parallelism: Belgae inhabit one, Aquitani another.
tokens.etymology: Connected with Aquitania, a region in southwestern Gaul.

tokens.contextMeaning: The third part of Gaul.
tokens.syntaxRole: Object in the final parallel clause.
tokens.grammarNote: Tertiam agrees with the understood partem.
tokens.etymology: From the same Indo-European base as tres.

tokens.contextMeaning: Introduces the people known by two names.
tokens.grammarNote: The relative pronoun agrees with the implied people in gender and number, while its nominative case comes from its role in the relative clause.
tokens.etymology: Part of the Latin relative/interrogative pronoun system.

tokens.contextMeaning: Contrasts their own language with Roman naming.
tokens.grammarNote: The genitive expresses whose language is meant.
tokens.etymology: Ipse is Latin's intensive pronoun: the very person or thing.

tokens.contextMeaning: In their own language.
tokens.grammarNote: The ablative can mark the respect in which a statement is true: by language/name.
tokens.etymology: Also means tongue; source of English linguistic.

tokens.contextMeaning: The name used in their own language according to Caesar.
tokens.grammarNote: With passive verbs of naming, Latin can use a nominative predicate name.
tokens.etymology: A classical ethnonym preserved in modern Celtic.

tokens.contextMeaning: In our Roman language.
tokens.grammarNote: The noun lingua is omitted but understood from the previous phrase.
tokens.etymology: From nos, we.

tokens.contextMeaning: The Roman name for the same people.
tokens.grammarNote: Latin pairs Celtae and Galli as alternative names under the passive verb appellantur.
tokens.etymology: Roman ethnonym behind Gallia and English Gaul.

tokens.contextMeaning: Names the people from two cultural perspectives.
tokens.grammarNote: The passive ending -ntur agrees with the plural relative subject qui.
tokens.etymology: From ad- plus a verb of addressing or naming.

cards.title: Gaul as evidence
cards.body: The opening makes geography serve rhetoric: Caesar defines the field before narrating the war.

cards.title: Belgae, Aquitani, Celtae
cards.body: The three groups are presented as distinct by territory, language, law, and custom.

cards.title: Roman classification
cards.body: The passage quietly turns local identities into a Roman administrative map.

timeline.event: Caesar begins his campaigns in Gaul.
The Gallic War is narrated in commentarii.
Vercingetorix leads the major revolt against Caesar.

passages.author: Cicero
passages.title: In Catilinam 1.1
passages.source: Public-domain Ciceronian text prepared as a hand-corrected MVP sample; intended to be replaceable by Perseus/Scaife CTS imports.
passages.description: Cicero opens with direct pressure: a sequence of questions turns grammar into courtroom momentum.

sentences.latin: Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?
sentences.translation: How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?
sentences.syntaxExplanation: Quo usque frames the question as a limit being exceeded. Abutere is a future or archaic passive-form deponent addressed directly to Catilina, while patientia nostra is the ablative object governed by abutor.

tokens.contextMeaning: Begins a question about how far Catiline will go.
tokens.grammarNote: Quo usque is an idiom meaning how long or to what limit.
tokens.etymology: Related to the qui/quis pronominal family.

tokens.contextMeaning: Intensifies the sense of a limit being crossed.
tokens.grammarNote: Together with quo it creates the famous opening challenge.
tokens.etymology: A Latin adverb of continuity or extension.

tokens.contextMeaning: Adds impatience and dramatic pressure.
tokens.grammarNote: In questions, tandem often carries emotional force: just how long, after all?
tokens.etymology: From tam plus a demonstrative/adverbial ending.

tokens.contextMeaning: Cicero accuses Catiline of exploiting public patience.
tokens.grammarNote: Abutor is deponent: passive in form, active in meaning. It commonly governs the ablative.
tokens.etymology: From ab- plus utor, to use; literally to use away or misuse.

tokens.contextMeaning: The accused conspirator addressed directly.
tokens.grammarNote: The vocative interrupts the question like a pointed finger in court.
tokens.etymology: Roman family name associated with Lucius Sergius Catilina.

tokens.contextMeaning: The endurance of Cicero and the state.
tokens.grammarNote: Some deponent verbs, including abutor, take an ablative complement where English expects a direct object.
tokens.etymology: From patior, to suffer or endure; source of English patience.

tokens.contextMeaning: Cicero speaks as consul and as voice of the Senate.
tokens.grammarNote: Nostra agrees with patientia in case, number, and gender.
tokens.etymology: From nos, we.

cards.title: Lucius Sergius Catilina
cards.body: A Roman aristocrat accused of plotting against the Republic after failed bids for the consulship.

cards.title: Senate under pressure
cards.body: The speech creates the feeling of an emergency hearing, with Catiline present as the target.

cards.title: Interrogation as attack
cards.body: Cicero does not begin by narrating facts. He begins by making delay itself seem intolerable.

timeline.event: The First Catilinarian is delivered in Rome.
